blocks.text: Magnus Huss coined 'alcoholism' in 1865, encompassing dependence, acute alcohol-related health issues and cumulative social problems. **ICD-10** has a diagnostic code for 'harmful use': actual physical/mental damage to the drinker without a dependence pattern.

**ICD-10** alcohol dependence requires >=3 of 7 in the last 12 months: intense desire to drink; difficulty controlling onset/termination/level; withdrawal symptoms; use of alcohol to relieve withdrawal; tolerance (dose escalation for same effect); salience (neglect of alternative pleasures); narrowing of the personal repertoire.

**DSM-IV** 'abuse' = maladaptive use despite social/occupational/physical/psychological problems, or use in hazardous situations, for at least one month (usually recurring over a longer period) - but not meeting dependence.

**DSM-IV** alcohol dependence requires >=3 of 7 for at least a month: consuming more/longer than intended; unsuccessful attempts to cut down; withdrawal symptoms; use to relieve withdrawal; tolerance (needs at least a ==50%== dose increase from baseline); salience (most time spent pursuing alcohol); failure of role obligations/physical health; giving up alternate pleasures; continued use despite known harm.

**DSM-5** merges 'abuse' and 'dependence' into a single Substance Use Disorder on a mild-to-severe continuum. Mild **SUD** needs 2-3 of 11 symptoms (vs **DSM-IV** abuse needing only 1). Craving was added; legal problems were removed (to reduce cultural variation). Gambling disorder is the only condition in the new 'behavioural addictions' category (previously an impulse control disorder in **DSM-IV**); internet gaming disorder and caffeine use disorder sit in **DSM-5** Section **III** pending further research.

**ICD-11** 'harmful pattern of use' requires damage to the user's physical/mental health or harm to others, evident over >=12 months if episodic or >=1 month if continuous (daily/almost daily) use. 'Hazardous substance use' carries increased risk but no identifiable harm yet and has no defined time period.

sections.title: 3. The Concept of Dependence — Tolerance, Withdrawal, Craving & Typologies

blocks.text: Tolerance has behavioural, pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic mechanisms. Withdrawal reactions inevitably co-occur when tolerance is due to increased neuronal excitability (depressants); tolerance from pharmacokinetic change may or may not produce withdrawal. Tolerance can occur even with intermittent use, but intermittent use is unlikely to cause withdrawal.
Regular benzodiazepine use causes marked withdrawal anxiety but comparatively little tolerance to anxiolytic effects (versus hypnotic effects) - the opposite pattern to barbiturates.

'Diminished/reversed tolerance' occurs: after a period of abstinence (tolerance reverts to normal, causing quick intoxication); in older patients with brain damage (curtailed neuroadaptation); in liver disease (mimics diminished tolerance); or idiosyncratically.

The pharmacology of reward differs from the pharmacology of withdrawal: cocaine produces modest withdrawal but very high reward potential. Compulsion (repetitive intense drug-seeking with an urge) differs from craving (a motivational state, occurring in withdrawal, with positive or negative emotional valence).

blocks.text: Seizure incidence in untreated alcohol-dependent patients is quoted as ==8%==, dropping to ==3%== if withdrawal is treated - attributed to a kindling process where repeated withdrawal episodes sensitise the brain to future seizures (true of withdrawal symptoms generally, not just seizures).

==30%== (not all) of patients with withdrawal seizures later develop delirium tremens (DTs). Risk factors for DTs/seizures: severe dependence, past history of DTs, older age, acute physical illness. Untreated DTs carry ~==10%== mortality. In polysubstance withdrawal including alcohol, alcohol withdrawal/DTs must be treated first given the mortality risk.

In around ==5%== of patients, delirium tremens sets in, with disturbed autonomic function (pulse/temperature/**BP** changes in either direction), clouded consciousness with hallucinations (often Lilliputian) and agitation.

Markers of excess alcohol consumption include raised **MCV** (macrocytosis), raised **GGT**, and carbohydrate-deficient transferrin (**CDT**); anaemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia and raised LFTs are also seen. Lactate dehydrogenase is **NOT** a recognised marker.

blocks.text: 'Opiate' refers only to natural opium alkaloids and semi-synthetics; 'opioid' is the broader term. Heroin is smoked ('chasing') most commonly, but can be injected, snorted or taken orally; street heroin is adulterated, so accidental injection of a purer batch can cause fatal toxicity. **UK** heroin prevalence is around ==1%== (male:female 2:1), most treatment-seekers in their 20s.

Three opioid receptors, all G-protein-coupled: Mu (most abused opioids are agonists here - analgesia, respiratory depression, euphoria in some, drowsiness, constipation, increased **VTA** dopamine release; tolerance develops to most Mu effects but little/none to constipation and miosis). Kappa agonists produce dysphoria, no pupillary effect, some analgesia, and decrease **VTA** dopamine release.

blocks.text: Morphine/heroin withdrawal ('cold turkey') begins 6-8 hours after last dose, peaks at 2 days, reduces over a week. Features: dysphoric mood, nausea/vomiting, muscle aches, lacrimation/rhinorrhea, pupillary dilation, piloerection, sweating, diarrhoea, yawning, fever, insomnia. Insomnia, bradycardia, temperature dysregulation and craving can persist for months, sometimes necessitating maintenance treatment.

Opioid withdrawal pupils are **DILATED**, not constricted - pupillary constriction is a feature of opioid **INTOXICATION**/overdose. This exact reversal is tested repeatedly across the question bank as 'which is **NOT**/least suggestive of opioid withdrawal'.

blocks.text: Benzodiazepine dependence risk rises steeply with duration of prescribed use: ==15%== dependent at 1-5 months of use, rising to nearly ==40%== at around a year (De las Cuevas 2003). Using prescribed benzodiazepines for 4 weeks or less rarely causes significant withdrawal; at 4 months 5-==10%== have withdrawal, at 2 years 25-==45%==, at 6-8 years ==75%== (Law et al. 2004).

Benzodiazepine dependence risk is duration-specific, not a flat figure: ~==15%== at 1-5 months of prescribed use but ~==40%== at around a year - the exam expects the correct number tied to the correct duration bucket, not just 'benzodiazepines cause dependence'.

blocks.text: Benzodiazepine overdose has a large safety margin versus barbiturates (lethal:effective dose ratio ~200:1 or higher); death, when it occurs (especially combined with alcohol/other sedatives), is usually from respiratory depression. **Flumazenil** is the specific benzodiazepine antagonist used in A&E/**ICU** to reverse effects.

Management of prescribed-benzodiazepine dependence: minimal interventions (advisory letters, brief relaxation) for early/mild dependence; graded discontinuation for established dependence (about ==66%== stop in the short term; long-term outcome unknown). Additional psychological therapies do not improve on graded discontinuation alone. **Buspirone**, antidepressants and anticonvulsants have repeatedly shown no meaningful added effect. **Carbamazepine** may substitute for benzodiazepines when controlling withdrawal from high illicit doses.

**GHB** has **GABA**-like action, inhibits dopamine release at low dose but boosts it on chronic use, and can induce noradrenaline release in the hypothalamus. Causes respiratory depression/coma (especially with alcohol) but the person may remain combative; bradycardia in 1/3 of users. **GHB** withdrawal resembles alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal, starting at 12 hours and lasting up to 12 days; routine toxicology screening does not detect **GHB**.

blocks.text: Amphetamines block catecholamine (dopamine/noradrenaline) reuptake and stimulate vesicular release - central sympathomimetics. Acute tolerance develops to subjective effects of d-amphetamine but not to its cardiopressor (hypertensive) effect in healthy subjects - meaning repeated dosing to maintain subjective effect can push plasma levels to toxic range (Brauer, Ambre & De Wit 1996).
Amphetamine withdrawal: dysphoric mood/'crash' (sometimes with suicidal ideation), fatigue, vivid unpleasant dreams, hypersomnia, increased appetite, psychomotor retardation, small pupils.

**MDMA** has two optical isomers: R(-) produces **LSD**-like effects via presynaptic serotonin release (irreversible long-term serotonergic damage -> depression risk); S(+) produces amphetamine-like effects. Lower doses are more stimulant-like, higher doses more hallucinogenic.

Cocaine is a potent dopamine-reuptake blocker; freebasing produces crack, which when smoked acts as rapidly as **IV** use. Faster absorption = more intense but shorter 'high': snorting yields a high lasting 15-30 minutes (slower onset), smoking/**IV** lasts only 5-10 minutes (rapid onset). At least ==60%== of cocaine users report mental health problems; ==18%== of these report psychotic experiences.

Cocaine route vs duration is counter-intuitive: snorting gives the **SLOWER**-onset but **LONGER**-lasting high (15-30 min), while smoking/**IV** gives the **FASTER**-onset but **SHORTER**-lasting high (5-10 min) - faster absorption means a more intense but shorter high, not a longer one.

blocks.text: Cocaine withdrawal is characterised by intense craving with a striking lack of physical withdrawal symptoms - dysphoria/crash, anhedonia, anxiety, irritability, hypersomnolence; usually resolves within 18 hours but can last up to a week (peaking at day 3) in heavy users.

Cocaine physical harms: nasal septal perforation (snorting), non-haemorrhagic cerebral infarction, subarachnoid/intraparenchymal/intraventricular haemorrhage, TIAs, seizures (3-==8%== of related A&E visits), **MI** and arrhythmias.

Caffeine is a methylxanthine, half-life 3-10 hours, antagonises adenosine receptors (raising intraneuronal cAMP); at high doses affects dopamine/noradrenergic neurons. A single low-moderate dose (20-200mg) increases alertness; 300-800mg produces unpleasant anxiety/nervousness. Caffeine causes global cerebral vasoconstriction (tolerance does not develop to this; rebound increase in blood flow on withdrawal) - except this may not occur over age 65.

**LSD** acts via sigma opioid, aspartate and serotonergic (5HT2A partial agonism) mechanisms; tolerance to sensory/psychological effects develops by the 2nd-3rd day of successive use, and 4-6 **LSD**-free days are needed to lose significant tolerance. Cross-tolerance exists among mescaline, psilocybin and **LSD**, but not between amphetamine and **LSD**. **LSD** carries no overdose risk and no physiological dependence/withdrawal.

Hallucinogen persisting perception disorder ('flashback phenomenon'): geometric hallucinations, false peripheral movement, colour flashes, trailing images, positive afterimages, halos, macropsia/micropsia, triggered by emotional stress, sensory deprivation or use of another psychoactive substance.

'Club drugs' (**NIDA**): **MDMA**, ecstasy, rohypnol, **GHB**, **ketamine**, **LSD**. **GHB**, flunitrazepam (rohypnol) and **ketamine** are 'date rape drugs' - strong sedation with amnesia, used for drugging/spiking.

Khat (Catha edulis leaves, chewed) contains cathinone, which shares most of amphetamine's **CNS**/peripheral actions; rapid buccal absorption and metabolism give low toxicity. Synthetic methcathinone is also used illicitly.

blocks.text: ==80%== of cigarette smokers are nicotine dependent. Cigarette-smoke polycyclic hydrocarbons induce hepatic **CYP1A2**, lowering blood levels (by up to ==50%==) of **clozapine**, **olanzapine**, **chlorpromazine**, **fluphenazine**, **haloperidol**, tricyclics, **mirtazapine**, **fluvoxamine** and **propranolol** - **lithium** is unaffected as it is renally cleared with no hepatic metabolism.

Nicotine withdrawal: dysphoric/depressed mood, insomnia, irritability/frustration/anger, anxiety, difficulty concentrating, restlessness, decreased heart rate, increased appetite/weight gain. Begins hours after last cigarette, peaks 2-3 days, eases over 1-3 weeks; cravings last longer. Mean post-cessation weight gain ~10 lb, greatest in women and heavy smokers.

Cannabis acts via the inhibitory Gi-linked **CB1** receptor (highest density in basal ganglia, hippocampus, cerebellum; sparse in cortex, none in brainstem - hence minimal respiratory/cardiac effect); **CB2** is peripheral/immune (spleen, thymus). Endogenous ligands are anandamides. Euphoria appears within minutes, peaks ~30 minutes, lasts 2-4 hours.

Cannabis withdrawal (irritability, insomnia, anorexia, mild nausea) is rare and occurs only after abrupt cessation of very high doses; evidence for physiological dependence is weak despite demonstrable tolerance and psychological dependence.

Inhalants (solvents, aerosol propellants, thinners, petrol) act as **CNS** depressants; effects appear within 5 minutes and last 30 minutes to several hours; blood concentration rises further if combined with alcohol. No dependence syndrome or reliable withdrawal syndrome is described. Signature exam clues: rashes around nose/mouth, unusual breath odour, ocular/oropharyngeal irritation. Chronic use can cause diffuse cerebral/cerebellar/brainstem atrophy and leukoencephalopathy.

sections.title: 9. Prescribing Controlled Drugs (Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001)

blocks.text: The Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001 create 5 schedules. Schedule 1 (coca leaf, cannabis, **LSD**, mescaline): no recognised medicinal use, Home Office licence needed to possess. Schedule 2 (diamorphine, morphine, pethidine, amphetamine, cocaine, secobarbital etc.): special prescription and safe-custody requirements, register required, destruction only witnessed.

Schedule 3 (barbiturates except secobarbital, **buprenorphine**, **temazepam**, pentazocine etc.): special prescription requirements but no safe-custody requirement (except **buprenorphine**, diethylpropion, flunitrazepam, **temazepam**) and no register - but invoices retained 2 years. blocks.text: **Clonidine**/lofexidine: presynaptic alpha-2 agonists reducing central sympathetic tone; opioid receptors on locus coeruleus projections reduce noradrenergic tone with long-term opioid use, and cellular adaptation (adenylate cyclase up-regulation) maintains sympathetic tone chronically - sudden opioid withdrawal causes increased adrenergic firing, which alpha-2 agonism counteracts.

Dexfenfluramine/fenfluramine cause massive serotonin release (Fen-Phen combination with phentermine was withdrawn for irreversible serotonergic damage, valvular regurgitation, pulmonary fibrosis). Levomethadyl acetate (**LAAM**) is a long-acting pure mu agonist, similar use to **methadone**, withdrawn due to **QT** prolongation/torsades de pointes.

**Varenicline** (Champix) is a partial agonist at the alpha4-beta2 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subunit - relieves nicotine withdrawal and reduces nicotine's rewarding properties. **Naloxone**: short-acting mu antagonist. **Naltrexone**: longer-acting mu antagonist. Phencyclidine: non-competitive **NMDA** antagonist (like **ketamine**), also binds sigma receptors.

**PCP** intoxication classically causes numbness/analgesia, nystagmus, ataxia and dysarthria - but seizures are **RARE**, making 'seizures' the correct answer to a 'least likely feature' question despite **PCP**'s reputation for causing severe agitation/violence.

blocks.text: Pathological (idiosyncratic) intoxication: severe behavioural reaction rapidly after a small amount of alcohol - confusion, hallucinations, high agitation, impulsive/aggressive behaviour, lasting hours and ending in prolonged sleep. Not coded in **DSM-5**; sometimes used as a forensic defence; may need physical restraint and **IM** **haloperidol**.

Alcoholic hallucinosis: alcohol-induced psychotic disorder, usually auditory hallucinations (unstructured sounds progressing to malign/threatening voices) with clear sensorium (unlike DTs), lasting usually <1 week; hallucinations >6 months should raise suspicion of an independent psychosis such as schizophrenia. Differentiators from schizophrenia: atypical/late onset, drinking clearly preceding onset, remission with abstinence, lack of thought disorder/affect incongruence. Responds well and rapidly to antipsychotics, though the evidence base is sparse.

Alcoholic hallucinosis is a recurring 'incorrect statement' **EMI**/**SBA** target: the exam repeatedly plants the false claim that its hallucinations 'cannot be treated with antipsychotics' or 'respond poorly to antipsychotics' - in fact persisting symptoms respond well to antipsychotics, and ==95%== resolve rapidly just with cessation of alcohol.

blocks.text: Alcoholic blackouts: discrete anterograde amnesia during intoxication (alcohol blocks hippocampal consolidation of new memories); remote memory is intact, complex tasks may still be performed but not later recalled; the gap usually lasts hours, rarely a day+. Not included in **DSM**/**ICD-10**.

Wernicke's encephalopathy (**WE**): triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, global confusion - but the classic triad is present in only ==10%== of patients, and ==80%== are undiagnosed before post-mortem. Caused by **thiamine** deficiency (poor intake, reduced **GI** absorption, decreased hepatic storage, impaired utilisation); a vulnerability related to abnormal **thiamine**-dependent transketolase may explain why not every **thiamine**-deficient alcoholic develops **WE**. Lesions (gliosis, small haemorrhages) cluster in mammillary bodies, hypothalamus, mediodorsal thalamic nucleus, colliculi, midbrain tegmentum - typically symmetrical.

**WE** seen in ~==12.5%== of chronic alcoholics in some series. **MRI** is the most valuable diagnostic tool: sensitivity only ==53%== but specificity ==93%== (Sechi & Serra 2007) - useful to confirm, not to exclude. Untreated/undertreated **WE** carries ~==20%== mortality and progresses to irreversible Korsakoff's syndrome in ==84%== of survivors. **Thiamine** must be given before **IV** glucose (glucose worsens **thiamine** deficiency biochemically).

Suspected/established **WE** - parenteral **thiamine** >500mg for 3-5 days (e.g. 2 pairs Pabrinex tds for 3 days, then 1 pair od for 3-5 days). Pabrinex also contains nicotinamide, pyridoxine (**B6**), riboflavin (**B2**) and vitamin C. Ophthalmoplegia responds within hours of treatment; cognitive impairment takes longer.

blocks.text: Korsakoff's syndrome (**KS**): ~==80%== of alcoholics recovering from **WE** later develop it; marked anterograde (and some retrograde) episodic memory deficit, apathy, intact sensorium, relatively preserved attention/procedural/working memory (digit span typically intact). Can occur without antecedent **WE** (repeated subclinical **WE** episodes may culminate in **KS**). Best correlates with dorsomedial thalamic lesions, though mammillary body/mammillothalamic tract/anterior thalamic lesions may matter more for memory. Confabulation reflects a double frontal + diencephalic lesion.

Cerebellar degeneration (Purkinje cell loss, 10-==35%==): reported in ~==40%== of chronic alcoholics; limb ataxia and dysarthria are more common than in **WE**, nystagmus is rare; many with **MRI** atrophy are not clinically ataxic; severity does not correlate directly with lifetime alcohol consumption; improves with abstinence.

Hepatocerebral degeneration: follows partial recovery from hepatic encephalopathy - tremor, choreoathetosis, dysarthria, gait ataxia, dementia, with astrocyte proliferation in basal ganglia/thalamus/red nucleus/pons/cerebellum without neuronal loss. Asterixis is a feature of **ACUTE** hepatic encephalopathy, not of hepatocerebral degeneration itself.

Marchiafava-Bignami syndrome: demyelination of the corpus callosum/adjacent white matter, first described (Carducci 1898) in Italian red wine drinkers, predominantly malnourished male alcoholics; ~250 cases reported in the literature (likely under-recognised). Type A: coma/stupor, pyramidal signs, whole callosum involved. Type B: normal/mild mental status, partial/focal callosal lesions (Heinrich 2004).

Central pontine myelinolysis: demyelination of the central base of the pons (Adams et al. 1959) - limb pain, bulbar palsy, quadriplegia, disordered eye movements, vomiting, confusion, coma/locked-in syndrome. Also occurs in non-alcoholic hyponatraemia (e.g. thiazide-induced) and other causes (Wilson's disease, malnutrition, burns, Addison's disease); can be induced experimentally by rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia.

Alcoholic pancreatitis-associated hypocalcaemia: pancreatic lipase releases free fatty acids that chelate calcium salts in the retroperitoneum (contributing to the back pain of pancreatitis); hypoalbuminaemia and hypomagnesaemia can compound it. **PTH** may be normal, suppressed, or elevated depending on severity. Treatment: parenteral calcium/magnesium replacement and vitamin D assessment.

blocks.text: Four models proposed to explain the high substance use disorder (**SUD**) rate in severe mental illness (**SMI**): common factor model (shared genetic/personality/social vulnerability - relatives of dual-diagnosis patients have more **SUD**, but relatives of substance-free **SMI** patients do not); secondary use model (self-medication of dysphoria/symptoms/social isolation); supersensitivity model (unusual sensitivity to substance-related harms triggers **SUD** diagnosis); secondary illness model (**SUD** causes mental illness via kindling/sensitisation - popular with lay public).

Stimulant-induced psychosis (mechanism: sensitisation) resembles schizophrenia but with: absence of prominent negative symptoms, predominance of visual hallucinations, generally appropriate affect, hyperactivity, disinhibited sexual behaviour, confusion/incoherence, almost no formal thought disorder. Diagnosis often rests on rapid resolution over days or a positive urine drug screen; treatment of choice is short-term antipsychotic (e.g. **haloperidol**).

Cannabis: 'hemp insanity' (florid psychosis) after high-potency high-dose use; cannabis rarely produces a hallucinogen-like 'bad trip'; long-term use may cause subtle cognitive impairment (memory, attention, integration of complex information); the 'amotivational syndrome' (apathy, anergia, weight gain) is controversial. Mild attentional problems/impulsivity are seen in children exposed to cannabis in utero.

Hallucinogen 'bad trip' resembles an acute panic reaction, occasionally with true psychotic symptoms; ends when acute effects wear off but course is variable. Flashback phenomenon (hallucinogen persisting perception disorder in **DSM-5**) can be triggered by emotional stress, sensory deprivation, or use of another psychoactive substance (alcohol/marijuana).

Chronic inhalant use: diffuse cerebral/cerebellar/brainstem atrophy with white matter disease (leukoencephalopathy) on **CT**/**MRI**; hearing loss, peripheral neuropathy, cerebellar signs, persisting motor impairment, parkinsonism, apathy, poor concentration, memory loss, visuospatial dysfunction, impaired linguistic processing, and (in some) lead encephalopathy.

blocks.text: ==40%== of the general population has a family history of alcoholism; 7-==9%== have multiple affected family members. **MZ** > **DZ** twin concordance; adoptee risk tracks the biological family (1.6-3.6x higher in adoptees-away of alcoholics); close family members have a 4-fold increased risk (Dawson 1992: odds up ~==167%==/~4x with both a 1st- and 2nd-degree affected relative, ~==86%==/~2x with one affected 1st-degree relative, ~==45%==/~1.5x with a 2nd/3rd-degree relative).

Virginia Adult Twin Study: heritability of alcohol use disorders 0.51-0.66. Males show higher familial tendency (50-==60%==) than females (25-==30%==) in some studies. Biomarkers: low 5HT/5-**HIAA**/**MAO** in impulsive problem drinkers; reduced **P300** amplitude in alcoholics **AND** their children; men with a family history show blunted cortisol/sway-test response to alcohol.

Key genetic loci: **ALDH2** variant (chromosome 12q24.2) - single base-pair change causing an Antabuse-like reaction; homozygous in ==12%== of South East Asian/Chinese people, conferring protection. **ADH2*2**/**ADH3*1** high-activity variants (chromosome 4q22) are significantly decreased in oriental alcohol-dependent populations (produce less acetaldehyde, more slowly). **DRD2** Taq1 polymorphism association is controversial and not widely believed.

blocks.text: **AUDIT**: sensitivity ==83%== (men)/==65%== (women) in primary care; **NICE**-recommended screening tool for non-specialist staff (GPs, acute/mental health staff), 10 items (**Q1-3** quantity, 4-6 dependence signs, 7-10 harm-related behaviours), max score 40, score >=8 suggests harmful/hazardous drinking. **FAST** is a shorter **AUDIT**-derived version for busy A&E settings.

**CAGE** is the most widely used screening tool but does **NOT** ask about frequency, quantity, or episodes of heavy drinking, so misses early problem drinking (Nilssen & Cone 1994); Aertgeerts et al. (2001) found **CAGE** sensitivity only ==62%== (men)/==54%== (women) in primary care.

blocks.text: Many alcohol withdrawal episodes occur without medical/pharmacological treatment; successive withdrawal episodes are associated with increasing severity/complications (kindling), including cognitive impairment.

Indications for inpatient (vs community) detoxification: past/current **DT** or seizure; psychiatric morbidity with suicide risk or debilitating physical health; **WE**/Korsakoff syndrome; homelessness/social difficulties likely to prevent completion. Community detox involves daily nurse contact for withdrawal assessment/monitoring.

Benzodiazepines outperform placebo across outcomes: severity reduction, reduced **DT**/seizure incidence, regimen completion/subsequent rehabilitation. Longer half-life benzodiazepines reduce delirium/seizure incidence more effectively but can accumulate in the elderly. Agents without phase-1 metabolism (**lorazepam**, **oxazepam**) suit patients with liver failure/**COPD** (though with more breakthrough-seizure risk and misuse potential).

Fixed regimen: **chlordiazepoxide** 20mg qds, reducing over ~7 days, with **PRN** titration in the first 2 days for uncomplicated withdrawal. 'Front-loading': a **diazepam** loading dose repeated every 90 minutes until light sedation, then no further dosing - **diazepam**'s long half-life covers withdrawal.

Symptom-triggered regimen: **chlordiazepoxide** given only when a validated scale (**CIWA**-Ar: 10 items, 10-20 moderate, >20 severe; or **SAWS**, self-completed, >12 needs treatment) shows significant symptoms. Advantage: faster control, fewer total doses, safer re over-sedation in intoxicated patients presenting for detox. Disadvantage: may undermine settings aiming to prevent symptoms altogether, and patient distress can reduce motivation.

Chlormethiazole is better avoided: higher respiratory depression risk than other benzodiazepines (especially with concurrent alcohol), variable bioavailability, higher addictive potential and street value.

**Carbamazepine** may be a first-line alternative to benzodiazepines - effective across the range of withdrawal severity, not contraindicated in liver failure - but has limited evidence for preventing DTs specifically. Anticonvulsants alone are as effective as benzodiazepines for seizures, but combining the two confers no extra benefit; **phenytoin** alone is ineffective for preventing a secondary withdrawal seizure, whereas **lorazepam** is effective.

**Haloperidol** reduces withdrawal signs/symptoms (meta-analysis) but does not reduce seizure/delirium risk as effectively as benzodiazepines, and may actually increase seizure likelihood versus placebo.

blocks.text: ==1 in 10== patients has spontaneous abstinence due to social change without formal relapse prevention. Factors favouring controlled drinking over total abstinence: age <40, early detection, minimal dependence, no medical/psychiatric complications, no impulsivity, stable social support, clear patient preference, and monitoring by partner/family being feasible.

**Acamprosate**: taurine derivative, inhibits glutamatergic **NMDA** function and rebalances **GABA**-glutamate imbalance, suppressing the 'urge to drink' in response to learned cues. **OR** for abstinence ~1.73 vs placebo (**NNT** 11 to prevent one relapse; **NNT** 8 for reduced craving). **GI** disturbance (nausea, diarrhoea) is the most common side effect. Should start as soon as possible after detox (delay reduces efficacy); benefit may persist 1-2 years after stopping. Not effective as monotherapy - always studied alongside psychosocial intervention. Combining with **disulfiram** improves outcome versus **acamprosate** alone.

**Naltrexone** (Adepend, **UK**-licensed 2012): mu-opioid antagonist, blocks alcohol-induced opioid release and reduces mesolimbic dopamine reward stimulation. Superior to placebo for abstinence maintenance, relapse rate, time to first drink, drinking days and **GGT** improvement; **OR** 1.46, **NNT** 9-11 as an adjunct to psychosocial intervention.

**Naltrexone** trials used 'time to relapse to heavy drinking' (>5 drinks/day or drinking >5 days/week) as the primary outcome, whereas **acamprosate** trials used complete abstinence - **naltrexone** therefore has evidence for reducing drinking/preventing a lapse becoming a full relapse rather than for maintaining total abstinence, and should **NOT** be stopped if drinking resumes (Volpicelli et al. 1997). Head-to-head, **naltrexone** and **acamprosate** show no difference on % abstinent or % retention.

**Naltrexone** and **acamprosate** are evidence-matched to **DIFFERENT** outcome measures: **naltrexone** trials use 'time to relapse to heavy drinking' (so it should not be stopped after a lapse), while **acamprosate** trials use complete abstinence as the endpoint - conflating the two outcome measures is a recurring higher-order trap in relapse-prevention SBAs.

**Nalmefene** (Selincro): opioid receptor modulator (antagonist at mu/delta, partial agonist at kappa), licensed for **REDUCING** consumption (not detox/abstinence). Uniquely can be started 'as needed' with no liver monitoring or prior detox required, initiated in community settings, for patients with a high drinking risk level (>60g/day men, >40g/day women per **WHO**) without physical withdrawal and not requiring immediate detox; must be combined with continuous psychosocial support and only initiated if the high-risk level persists 2 weeks after initial assessment.

**Disulfiram** inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, causing acetaldehyde accumulation (flushing, nausea, vomiting, headache, tachycardia, palpitations) if alcohol is taken - a dose-dependent reaction that can progress to hypertension, collapse, even death with larger amounts. It acts as a deterrent, not aversion (aversion uses agents like valeric acid/apomorphine paired with alcohol to create nausea directly). Witnessed/supervised dosing improves efficacy; reduces drinking days/quantity but does not itself increase abstinence rates; typical duration 3-6 months or as long as benefit continues. Contraindications: impulsivity, psychosis, suicidality, severe hepatic dysfunction, peripheral neuropathy, cardiac disease.

blocks.text: Project **MATCH** (9-centre **USA** **RCT**, n=1726) tested matching **CBT**/Twelve-Step Facilitation (**TSF**)/Motivational Enhancement Therapy (**MET**) to client characteristics across parallel outpatient and aftercare arms - little evidence that matching improved overall outcome. **AA** attendance predicted better long-term outcome, especially without a non-drinking support network. At 1 year, low-psychiatric-severity clients did better on abstinent days with **TSF** than **CBT**; at 3 years, clients with drinking-supportive social networks benefited more from **TSF**, those with low drinking support benefited more from **MET**. Readiness-to-change and self-efficacy were the strongest predictors of long-term outcome.

**UKATT** (7-centre **UK** pragmatic **RCT**, n=742, ==83%== 1-year follow-up) compared Motivational Enhancement Therapy with Social Behaviour and Network Therapy (**SBNT** - 8 sessions of 50 minutes, drawing on network therapy, behavioural marital therapy, unilateral family therapy, community reinforcement, relapse prevention, social skills training). **SBNT** did not differ significantly in effectiveness from **MET**.

Slattery et al. (2003) meta-analysis: **CBT**, behavioural self-control training (**BSCT**), **MET**, coping skills training and marital/family therapy all showed similar, moderate-to-small beneficial effect sizes.

Behavioural self-control training (**BSCT**): limiting drinks, self-monitoring/drink diary, non-alcoholic spacers, food before/after drinking, altering drinking rate, assertiveness to refuse offers, self-reward for reaching goals, developing awareness of antecedents and alternate coping.
**FRAMES**: Feedback of risks; Responsibility highlighted; Advice to abstain/cut down; Menu of alternative options/activities; Empathic interviewing; Self-efficacy enhanced throughout.

blocks.text: Twelve-step facilitation (e.g. **AA**): the **AA** model holds that once someone becomes an alcoholic they remain so, encouraging continuous vigilance/lifestyle change. Expert consensus: introduce and encourage but do **NOT** mandate **AA** attendance - compulsion reduces **AA**'s efficacy.

Motivational interviewing (Miller): directive, patient-centred, based on the transtheoretical model of change, aiming to create dissonance until the patient considers alternatives. Four principles: express empathy (reflective listening); develop attitude-behaviour discrepancy; sidestep/roll with resistance without confrontation; support self-efficacy for change.

Prochaska & DiClemente's transtheoretical model of change: precontemplation -> contemplation -> determination/preparation -> action -> maintenance (with relapse possible at any stage, feeding back into the cycle).

Six-stage transtheoretical model trap: the question bank's **EMI** adds a 'Ready for action' stage (planning/goal-setting/self-evaluation) distinct from both 'Preparation' and 'Action' - candidates trained only on the standard 5-stage precontemplation/contemplation/preparation/action/maintenance model can mis-map this vignette.

blocks.text: Suboxone (**buprenorphine** + **naloxone**, 4:1 ratio): **naloxone** has negligible effect sublingually but produces unpleasant withdrawal if injected by opioid-dependent users - deterring **IV** misuse; can still produce an agonist 'high' if injected by a **NON**-dependent person. Approved by the European regulator.

**Naltrexone** for opioid relapse prevention: long-acting (72h) mu antagonist, nullifying heroin's effect if a lapse occurs. Evidence base for effectiveness is currently inadequate; may help highly motivated patients or those fearing severe consequences of relapse (e.g. healthcare professionals). Implants/depots are untested in Phase **III** RCTs and not currently recommended. Side effects: insomnia, anxiety, nervousness, dysphoria, abdominal pain/cramps, nausea/vomiting, low energy, joint/muscle pain, headache, depression. Can precipitate serious withdrawal if given to an ongoing heroin user.

**Naltrexone** in opioid dependence carries two distinct traps: its relapse-prevention efficacy evidence is explicitly **INCONCLUSIVE** (not proven, not disproven), and it can precipitate a severe withdrawal reaction if given without an adequate opioid-free 'wash-out' period - both facts are tested as standalone 'true statement' items.

blocks.text: **NICE** opioid detoxification summary: offer detox readily with full information (including loss of tolerance and consequent intoxication risk after successful detox); offer community-based detox routinely **EXCEPT** after previous failed community detox, significant additional physical/mental health problems, polydrug detox, or considerable social problems; offer **buprenorphine** or **methadone** first-line per patient preference, normally continuing the same drug used for maintenance; consider lofexidine especially for mild/uncertain dependence (warn that adjuncts are needed for nausea/vomiting/shivering) - lofexidine detox outcomes are no better than **buprenorphine**/**methadone**; do **NOT** routinely use benzodiazepines, minor analgesics or antidiarrhoeals for opioid withdrawal.

**NICE** psychosocial recommendations: opportunistic brief interventions for those in limited contact with services; routine information on self-help groups (12-step, e.g. Narcotics/Cocaine Anonymous); contingency management with vouchers/privileges contingent on drug-negative tests, starting around £2-3 ($4) and escalating with continuous abstinence. Urine testing schedule: 3x/week for first 3 weeks, 2x/week for next 3 weeks, then weekly until stable.

Injectable diamorphine maintenance is an option for patients who fail to respond adequately to oral opioid substitution (**methadone** then **buprenorphine**); the prescriber needs a Home Office licence, and it is delivered as part of a holistic package with adjunctive psychosocial support, typically supervised twice daily at a specialist facility. Slow-release oral morphine and dihydrocodeine are **NOT** licensed in the **UK** for opioid dependence treatment.

Opiate-using mothers: **OR** for antepartum haemorrhage 2.33; mean birthweight reduction ~500g with heroin/**methadone** use; also microcephaly and neonatal withdrawal risk. sections.title: 19. Treatments for Other Substances & Smoking Cessation

blocks.text: Amphetamine dependence: most users do not become dependent, but dependence/craving can develop rapidly in some. Pharmacological evidence is weak; **CBT** and contingency management are the main recommended treatments (poor-quality evidence). Amineptine showed favourable **RCT** results but was withdrawn for abuse potential.

Cocaine withdrawal: no pharmacological agent reliably reduces intensity/craving. Dopamine agonists (amantadine, bromocriptine, pergolide) show no significant benefit in meta-analysis; evidence does not support dopamine agonists, antidepressants, **carbamazepine** or **olanzapine** for cocaine dependence.

Contingency management: tangible positive reinforcers (e.g. vouchers exchangeable for goods/services) for objective evidence of behaviour change (e.g. drug-negative urine). The 'fish-bowl procedure' lets patients draw a voucher worth $1-$100 after each negative test. **RCT**-supported for maintaining cocaine abstinence (Higgins 2003) and for cocaine abstinence in **methadone**-maintained opioid addicts (Rawson 2002, effect seen for cocaine not opioid abstinence). **NICE** recommends contingency management for primary stimulant misuse and for illicit drug use during **methadone** maintenance - it has the most consistent evidence base of any psychosocial intervention for these groups. Main limitation: response reduces/is lost once reinforcement stops.

Smoking cessation: 6+ months abstinence is the accepted trial outcome; without assistance only 5-==10%== of quit attempts succeed long-term. **NRT** increases 6-month abstinence (**OR** 1.74, meta-analysis of 96 RCTs); given for up to 2 weeks after quitting in the book notes, though **NICE**-era practice in the question bank cites an 8-12 week initial course (up to 9 months if cravings persist). All **NRT** formulations (gum, patch, inhaler, nasal spray, sublingual tablet, lozenge) are similarly efficacious but differ in compliance: patch ==82%==, gum ==38%==, nasal spray ==15%==, inhaler ==11%== compliant in week 1. Combining products (e.g. patch + inhalator) can be more effective; higher-dose products suit heavily dependent smokers.

**NRT** delivery speed: nasal spray fastest (peak blood nicotine at 5-10 min); patch slowest but most constant (16-24h); gum/inhaler peak at ~20 min via oral/pharyngeal mucosa. None matches the speed of smoking itself. **NRT** is safe in stable cardiac disease (safer than smoking); evidence is insufficient in pregnancy and under-18s (case-by-case). Some smokers transfer dependence onto **NRT** itself.

**Bupropion**: not licensed for adolescents or pregnant women; contraindicated with a history of seizures or eating disorders. Anti-smoking effect is independent of past depression history. Dosed 150mg/day for 6 days then increased to 300mg/day; smoking must stop by day 8; total course 8 weeks. Adding a nicotine patch to **bupropion** was not significantly better than **bupropion** alone.

**NICE**: if a quit attempt with **NRT** or **bupropion** fails, do not usually re-prescribe either within 6 months. Other agents with some evidence: **nortriptyline**; oral/transdermal **clonidine** (Gourlay & Benowitz 1995, inconsistent trial results). **Varenicline** (alpha4-beta2 nicotinic partial agonist) relieves withdrawal and reduces nicotine's rewarding effect.
Methamphetamine is **NOT** among the **UK** **NICE**/licensed first-line stop-smoking medications (**NRT**, **varenicline**, **bupropion**) - a recurring 'odd one out' style question.

Linked to dopamine-transmission genetic markers and impulsive personality traits.

Gambling disorder pharmacotherapy: **naltrexone** (especially higher doses) has meaningful efficacy in 2 favourable RCTs; SSRIs have mixed evidence (**fluvoxamine** 1 favourable/1 negative **RCT**; **citalopram** 1 favourable open-label; **sertraline** 1 negative **RCT**); **lithium** has 2 favourable RCTs. Psychological treatment has high drop-out though **CBT** looks promising (George & Murali 2007).

Internet addiction (Young, 1998; **DSM-5** research appendix, not a formal diagnosis): five types - cybersexual addiction, cyberrelationship addiction, net compulsion (gambling/shopping), information overload (compulsive database searching), computer/gaming addiction. Reported more often in China, Taiwan, and Southeast Asia than Europe/Americas.

Compulsive buying ('oniomania'): not a recognised **DSM**/**ICD** disorder; defined (Murali et al. 2012) as uncontrollable, distressing/time-consuming/impairing buying not occurring only during hypomania/mania. Estimated prevalence 2-==8%==, >==80%== female in survey samples; ==68%== lifetime prevalence of any affective disorder (mostly depression). SSRIs (high-dose **citalopram**/**escitalopram**, open-label) and **CBT** with self-monitoring (**RCT** evidence) have shown benefit.

Anabolic steroids: Class C under the Misuse of Drugs Act, but **ICD-10** classifies steroid abuse as a non-psychoactive substance disorder (**F50**.xx, alongside hormones) rather than an addiction (F1x.xx). Up to ==13%== exposure in some fitness-centre surveys; doses used are 10-100x therapeutic/physiological levels. Patterns: 'cycling' (4-12 weeks cyclical use), 'stacking' (multiple preparations concurrently), 'pyramiding' (dose escalated to a peak then tapered). Associated with aggression/'roid rage', violence, psychosis, mania, depression, and endocrine effects (acne ~==50%==, testicular atrophy/gynaecomastia in ~1/3).

'Legal highs'/novel psychoactive substances (book notes era, pre-blanket-ban): 5-==10%== of young Europeans used a legal high in the previous year vs 25-==50%== for cannabis (Gallup 2011). Testing a novel psychoactive product for harm cost ~£1 million and took ~1 year, making it practically impossible to legislate ahead of new products. Categories: stimulant-like (mephedrone/'meow meow' etc. - **SERT**/**DAT**/**NAT** blockade, risk of serotonin syndrome/psychosis/hyperthermia), psychedelic-like (**DMT**, Salvia - 5HT/**D2** receptor activity), cannabis-like ('Spice' - **CB1**/**CB2** agonists), benzomimetic (phenazepam etc. - **GABA** facilitation, respiratory depression risk), dissociative (methoxetamine etc. - **NMDA** antagonism).

Gambling pharmacotherapy: **naltrexone** (especially higher doses) and **lithium** each have 2 favourable RCTs; SSRIs show mixed evidence.

Internet addiction (not a formal **DSM-5** diagnosis, research appendix only) has 5 types: cybersexual, cyberrelationship, net compulsion, information overload, gaming — reported more often in China/Taiwan/**SE** Asia than Europe/Americas.

Anabolic steroids are Class C under the Misuse of Drugs Act, but **ICD-10** classifies steroid abuse as a non-psychoactive substance disorder (**F50**.xx) rather than an addiction (F1x.xx); patterns include cycling, stacking, and pyramiding.
Legal highs/**NPS**: testing a novel psychoactive product for harm cost ~£1 million and took ~1 year, making legislation practically impossible to keep ahead of new products.

Compulsive buying: ==68%== lifetime prevalence of any affective disorder (mostly depression); high-dose **citalopram**/**escitalopram** (open-label) and **CBT** with self-monitoring (**RCT** evidence) show benefit.
Anabolic steroid endocrine effects: acne in ~==50%==, testicular atrophy/gynaecomastia in ~1/3; associated with aggression/'roid rage', violence, psychosis, mania, depression.

sections.title: 21. Pregnancy: Alcohol, Other Drugs & Neonatal Withdrawal

blocks.text: Foetal alcohol syndrome is the commonest non-genetic cause of learning disability - intellectual impairment, dysmorphic facial features, disruptive behaviour. Advice: do not drink in pregnancy (or at most one drink/day per the book notes; current **UK** guidance is zero units/week). Psychosocial intervention is the mainstay of treatment; symptomatic withdrawal needs medically covered (ideally inpatient) detox. **Disulfiram**, **acamprosate** and **naltrexone** should be **AVOIDED** in pregnancy for maintaining abstinence.

Neonatal withdrawal features by substance: alcohol - hyperactivity, crying, irritability, poor sucking, tremors, seizures, poor sleep, hyperphagia, diaphoresis, within 3-12h of delivery (**FAS** features may emerge later). Opiates - onset 24-48h (occasionally delayed to 3-4 days), hyperirritability, **GI** dysfunction, respiratory distress, autonomic signs, tremor, high-pitched cry, loose stools; **methadone** withdrawal typically 48-72h post-birth (can be delayed to 3 weeks), milder with **buprenorphine**. Nicotine - mild fine tremor/tone changes, poor self-regulation. Marijuana - mild opiate-like syndrome, fine tremor, hyperacusis, prominent Moro reflex, rarely needing treatment. Amphetamines/cocaine - withdrawal itself unclear, but linked to prematurity and intrauterine growth restriction. Antidepressants - jitteriness, respiratory distress; more common with short-acting SSRIs (e.g. **paroxetine**) than **sertraline**.
